items.s: Passes through gains to investors but never passes through losses.
items.w: REITs pass through gains only; any losses show up as a lower share price on the exchange.

items.s: Passes through both passive gains and passive losses to investors.
items.w: DPPs flow income, gains, losses and deductions to partners, which is why they can act as tax shelters.

items.s: Investing in it offers no tax shelter benefit because losses are not passed through.
items.w: Unlike direct real estate ownership or a DPP, a REIT does not pass losses to investors, so no shelter.

items.s: Losses received may be used only to offset passive gains, not ordinary income or capital gains.
items.w: The passive-loss limitation applies to DPP investors: passive losses can only offset passive gains.

items.s: Dividends are always taxed as ordinary income at the investor’s own tax bracket.
items.w: REIT dividends never get the lower qualified-dividend rate that traditional corporate dividends can receive.

items.s: Generally appropriate only for institutional and accredited investors because of high risk and illiquidity.
items.w: DPPs often operate as blind pools with no guaranteed secondary market, so only sophisticated investors suit them.

items.s: Must distribute at least 90% of taxable income to shareholders each year to keep pass-through status.
items.w: The 90% annual distribution requirement is one of the three IRS tests applied to REITs.

items.s: Has potentially unlimited personal liability for the debts of the partnership.
items.w: The general partner actively manages the business and so carries unlimited personal liability for partnership debts.

items.s: Liability is limited to the amount invested in the partnership.
items.w: Limited partners trade a passive role for protection of personal assets beyond their ownership interest.

items.s: Stands last in line, behind limited partners, when assets are distributed on dissolution.
items.w: Liquidation order is secured lenders, general creditors, limited partners, then general partners last.

items.s: Has the right to inspect the books and records and to sue the managing partner for acting against the partnership’s interest.
items.w: Inspection and the right to sue the general partner are listed rights of limited partners.

items.s: Has the right to accept or reject new limited partners and to bind the partnership in contracts.
items.w: Accepting new limited partners and binding the partnership are management rights held by the general partner.

items.s: May vote on admitting a new general partner or on the sale of partnership property.
items.w: This infrequent voting right is called partnership democracy and belongs to limited partners, not to management.

items.s: Owes a fiduciary responsibility to act in the best interest of the limited partners.
items.w: Because the general partner invests the capital and runs the partnership, it carries fiduciary responsibility.

items.s: Registered under the ’33 Act and subject to a prospectus and annual and quarterly reports.
items.w: Public non-traded REITs are registered securities with SEC disclosure filings, unlike private-placement REITs.

items.s: Sold only to accredited investors and institutional clients.
items.w: Private REITs are exempt from registration and restricted to accredited investors and institutions.

items.s: Generally exempt from SEC registration and the related disclosure requirements.
items.w: Private or private-placement REITs avoid registration, which is why they lack disclosure documents.

items.s: Distributed through broker-dealers, with early redemption limited and holding periods of eight years or more not uncommon.
items.w: Non-traded REITs are public offerings sold through broker-dealers, but their shares are generally illiquid.

items.s: Lack of disclosure documents makes it hard for investors to make an informed decision.
items.w: Without registration there is no prospectus, so informed analysis is difficult for private REIT buyers.

items.s: Registered securities that are simply not listed on any exchange.
items.w: The registration table shows non-traded REITs as registered but not exchange-listed, while private ones are neither.

items.s: Neither registered under the ’33 Act nor listed on an exchange.
items.w: The book’s table gives private REITs a No for registration and a No for exchange listing.

items.s: Is an unsecured debt instrument, typically issued by a broker-dealer.
items.w: An ETN is unsecured corporate debt backed by its issuer, not a pool of securities.

items.s: Actually owns the securities held in its portfolio.
items.w: ETFs own their portfolio securities, whereas ETNs only track the performance of an underlying security.

items.s: Credit quality depends on the creditworthiness of the issuing bank, not the underlying asset.
items.w: ETN investors face issuer default risk because the note is a debt obligation of the sponsor.

items.s: Has a maturity date at which the instrument is liquidated.
items.w: Because it is a note, an ETN matures, which is a feature an ETF does not have.

items.s: Has a deeper secondary market and is more liquid.
items.w: The secondary market for ETNs is much more limited, so ETFs are the more liquid product.

items.s: Suitable for a wider range of investors because it tracks an index without complex products.
items.w: ETFs are simpler and track an index, making them more suitable than ETNs for most investors.

items.s: Combines a bond that protects principal with a derivative that provides equity exposure.
items.w: This structure describes the ETN: most of the investment is a bond and the remainder a derivative.

items.s: Usually carries a lock-up period of two years or more.
items.w: Hedge funds are highly illiquid and often impose lock-ups that prevent withdrawals for extended periods.

items.s: Can be redeemed with the issuer, so it is highly liquid.
items.w: Mutual fund shares can be redeemed with the issuer, in contrast to the illiquidity of hedge funds.

items.s: May invest in non-securities such as real estate and jewelry.
items.w: Hedge funds have broad authority to hold non-securities and tangible investments in addition to securities.

items.s: Has only a limited ability to trade on margin.
items.w: Mutual funds are restricted in margin use, while hedge funds generally take on significant leverage.

items.s: Expense ratio is usually about 1% or less.
items.w: Hedge funds charge about a 2% management fee plus a share of profits, far above a typical mutual fund.

items.s: Exempt from the Investment Company Act of 1940, giving more flexibility in structure.
items.w: Hedge funds are exempt from the ’40 Act, whereas mutual funds are regulated under it.

items.s: Generally takes on significant leverage, including through derivatives.
items.w: Significant leverage and derivatives are characteristic of hedge funds and not of mutual funds.

items.s: Offered to the public and traded on exchanges.
items.w: A master limited partnership is a limited partnership that is publicly traded on exchanges.

items.s: Does not generally trade on an exchange.
items.w: Regular limited partnerships lack an active exchange market, which makes them less liquid than other products.

items.s: Considered more liquid and less risky than other DPP investments.
items.w: Exchange trading makes the MLP more liquid and therefore less risky than other DPP investments.

items.s: Generally suitable only for institutional and sophisticated investors.
items.w: Like other DPPs, a regular LP carries high risk and illiquidity that limits it to sophisticated investors.

items.s: Interests are freely transferable, much like shares of a corporation.
items.w: Free transferability of interests is one of the advantages MLPs offer over ordinary limited partnerships.

items.s: Offers no guarantee that a secondary market will exist for resale of the interest.
items.w: DPPs without exchange listing have no guaranteed secondary market, unlike exchange-traded MLP interests.

items.s: Appropriate for a wider range of investors, including retail investors.
items.w: Because MLPs are exchange-traded, they suit retail investors and not just institutional or accredited investors.
